Almost every executive I work with has the same moment. After three or four months, they come to a session and say: I've stopped improving. And I understand the feeling. At the beginning, progress is easy to see. You learn fifty words, you use them the next day. Then the easy progress is over, and what is left is harder to notice: speed, confidence, the words that come without thinking. So you plateau, or you think you do. Most of the time the feeling is wrong. So I give them three tips. First, record yourself once a month, and compare. The difference you cannot feel, you can hear. Second, do one thing every week that is outside your comfort zone. And third, set one stretch goal at a time. Not five. One.

When I went to my first conferences in English, I used to hide. Really. I used to sit at the back of the room, check my phone at every coffee break, and leave before the dinner, because the dinner was where people actually talked. That was about ten years ago, at a bank in Mexico City. Today I'm used to starting conversations with strangers, and I'm used to presenting numbers on a panel. That took a few years. I'm still getting used to jokes in English, and to some very fast accents. But here's my advice. Don't wait until you feel ready. Nobody feels ready. You get used to it by doing it, one conversation at a time.
